hints: Look at the relative positions of the two ethyl groups on the benzene ring in E and recall how 1,2, 1,3 and 1,4 relate to ortho, meta and para.
walkthrough:
Identify the parent and substituents**
You have a benzene ring with two identical $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ groups. The parent is benzene and each substituent is ethyl, so the name will be diethylbenzene with numbers to show positions.

Number to show the relationship**
In E the groups are separated by one ring carbon, that is the meta relationship. Numbering to give the lowest set gives positions 1 and 3, so the systematic name is 1,3-diethylbenzene.

hints: Think about why a normal proton containing solvent would ruin a proton NMR spectrum and what type of solvent avoids this.
walkthrough:
Remember what the spectrometer sees**
Proton NMR detects $^{1}\text{H}$ nuclei. If you dissolve your sample in a solvent that contains lots of $^{1}\text{H}$, like $\text{CHCl}_3$ or water, the huge solvent signal would swamp the small sample signals.

Choose an invisible solvent**
Deuterium, $^{2}\text{H}$ or D, resonates at a completely different frequency, so it is invisible in the $^{1}\text{H}$ spectrum. $\text{CDCl}_3$ dissolves most organic compounds well and contains no $^{1}\text{H}$, plus it provides the lock signal, so it is the standard choice.

hints: Recall which types of proton disappear after shaking with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ and check whether hydrocarbon E contains any of them.
walkthrough:
Recall what D2O does**
Shaking with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ only affects labile protons, that is $\text{O-H}$ in alcohols, phenols and carboxylic acids and $\text{N-H}$ in amines and amides. The reaction $\text{R-O-H} + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-O-D} + \text{HOD}$ replaces $^{1}\text{H}$ with invisible D, so that signal vanishes.

Apply to E**
E is $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$, a hydrocarbon containing only $\text{C-H}$ bonds on alkyl groups and the aromatic ring. There is no $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$ to exchange, so both spectra are identical.
Final answer: No difference / no peak disappears because E is a hydrocarbon with no labile $\text{O-H}$, $\text{N-H}$ proton that can exchange with D.

hints: Use Table 7.2 to match the delta values 1.3, 2.7 and 7.1 to alkane, alkyl next to aromatic ring, and aromatic proton environments.
Count equivalent protons in 1,2-diethylbenzene to work out the integration ratio for the two ethyl groups versus the ring.
Apply the n+1 rule to the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ fragment to predict triplet versus quartet splitting.
walkthrough:
Assign the environments from chemical shift**
Table 7.2 tells you $\delta$ 0.9 to 1.7 is alkane $\text{-CH}_3$, $\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$, $\delta$ 2.3 to 3.0 is alkyl next to aromatic ring $\text{CH}_3\text{-Ar}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{-Ar}$, and $\delta$ 6.0 to 9.0 is $\text{H-Ar}$. So 1.3 must be the $\text{CH}_3$ away from the ring, 2.7 must be the benzylic $\text{CH}_2$ attached directly to the ring, and 7.1 must be the aromatic protons.

Use symmetry for integration**
In D the two ethyl groups are equivalent by symmetry. That gives $2 \times 3 = 6$ equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ protons and $2 \times 2 = 4$ equivalent $\text{CH}_2$ protons. The disubstituted ring has $6 - 2 = 4$ aromatic protons. The ratio 6:4:4 matches the peak areas in Fig. 7.2.

Apply n+1 to the ethyl group**
For $\text{Ar-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$, the $\text{CH}_3$ sees 2 neighbours on $\text{CH}_2$, so $n+1 = 2+1 = 3$, a triplet at $\delta$ 1.3. The $\text{CH}_2$ sees 3 neighbours on $\text{CH}_3$, so $n+1 = 3+1 = 4$, a quartet at $\delta$ 2.7. This is exactly what Fig. 7.2 shows.
Final answer: delta 1.3: 6 H, $\text{CH}_3$, triplet; delta 2.7: 4 H, $\text{CH}_2$, quartet; delta 7.1: 4 H, aromatic $\text{H-Ar}$.

hints: Draw D (1,2) and E (1,3) and look for a mirror plane that makes carbons equivalent, remembering to include the alkyl carbons.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbons using symmetry**
Think in terms of symmetry, not total carbons. For D, 1,2-diethylbenzene, the two ethyl groups are equivalent, giving one $\text{CH}_3$ type and one $\text{CH}_2$ type. On the ring, $\text{C}1 = \text{C}2$, $\text{C}3 = \text{C}6$, $\text{C}4 = \text{C}5$, giving 3 ring types. Total $= 2 + 3 = 5$.
For E, 1,3-diethylbenzene, the ethyl groups are still equivalent, giving one $\text{CH}_3$ and one $\text{CH}_2$ type. On the ring, $\text{C}1 = \text{C}3$, $\text{C}4 = \text{C}6$, with $\text{C}2$ and $\text{C}5$ unique, giving 4 ring types. Total $= 2 + 4 = 6$. More symmetry in D means fewer peaks, so $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR distinguishes them.
Final answer: D has 5 peaks; E has 6 peaks.

hints: Write the molecular formulae of D ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$) and F (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid) first, then balance C and H with $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Work out the formulae and balance**
D is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2 = \text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$. F is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2 = \text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{4}$. Each ethyl side chain is oxidised, with one carbon retained as $\text{COOH}$ and one carbon lost as $\text{CO}_2$. Balancing C: $10 = 8 + 2$, so $2\text{CO}_2$. Balancing H: $14 = 6 + 2 \times$ H in water, so $4\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Balancing O then needs 12 atoms of [O]: $$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14} + 12[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{4} + 2\text{CO}_{2} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Recall what $\text{SOCl}_2$ does to a $\text{COOH}$ group and apply it to both $\text{COOH}$ groups in the 1,2-diacid F.
Think about how one molecule of ethane-1,2-diol can bridge the two adjacent $\text{COCl}$ groups to form a cyclic product J.
For K with formula $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{12}\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_6$, consider linking two molecules of G with one diol where only one $\text{COCl}$ on each ring reacts.
walkthrough:
Form G, the diacyl chloride**
$\text{SOCl}_2$ in excess converts each $\text{-COOH}$ to $\text{-COCl}$ with loss of $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$. Since F is the 1,2-diacid, G is simply the 1,2-diacyl chloride: a benzene ring with $\text{C(=O)Cl}$ in both the 1 and 2 positions, formula $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$. Keep the ortho relationship, it is crucial for what follows.

Form J, the intramolecular cyclic diester**
Acyl chlorides react readily with alcohols to give esters. One $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ molecule has two $\text{OH}$ groups perfectly placed to react with the two adjacent $\text{COCl}$ groups on the same G molecule, closing a new ring. The product J is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}(\text{COOCH}_{2})_{2}$ cyclic, formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{4}$, with a $\text{-COO-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-OOC-}$ bridge between C1 and C2 of the benzene.

Form K, the 2:1 intermolecular product**
If instead one diol reacts with two separate G molecules, using one $\text{OH}$ per G and leaving one $\text{COCl}$ unreacted on each ring, you get K. Its formula $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{12}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{O}_{6}$ equals $2 \times$ G plus diol minus $2\text{HCl}$. Draw two 1,2-disubstituted rings linked by $\text{-COO-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-OOC-}$ in the centre, with a $\text{COCl}$ remaining ortho to each ester linkage on each ring.

Final answer: G: benzene-1,2-dicarbonyl dichloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COCl})_2$ with $\text{COCl}$ groups in 1,2 positions; J: cyclic ester $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COO})_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$, ethylene bridge linking 1 and 2 positions; K: $\text{ClOC-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COO-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-OOC-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COCl}$ with 1,2 substitution on each ring.
